pageTitle: Reverb Pedals: Spring Tanks, Plate Shimmer, Convolution & Acoustic Space
subtitle: The acoustic dimension of tone — physical electromechanical spring tanks, studio plates, DSP algorithmic halls & ethereal ambient shimmer

introduction.title: Reverb Pedals: Spring Tanks, Plate Shimmer, Convolution & Acoustic Space
introduction.text:
Every sound in nature occurs within a physical space. When you pluck an acoustic guitar in a tiled bathroom or a vaulted cathedral, sound waves radiate outward, bouncing off walls, floors, and ceilings thousands of times per second. These thousands of micro-reflections blend into a smooth, dense, decaying wash of acoustic energy known as reverberation. Without reverb, an electric guitar signal fed directly from a magnetic pickup sounds unnatural, dry, and flat—as if plucked inside an anechoic isolation chamber. Reverb is the acoustic environment your guitar inhabits.

The history of artificial reverb is a story of ingenious acoustic and electronic engineering. In the 1960s, Leo Fender popularized the electromechanical spring reverb tank—driving physical steel springs with an electromagnetic transducer to create the splashy, drippy, percussive sound of surf rock. In recording studios, German engineers suspended massive 600-pound cold-rolled steel plates (the EMT 140) to produce dense, silky high-frequency decay for vocal and guitar tracks. Today, advanced 32-bit floating-point Digital Signal Processors (DSP) solve complex feedback delay networks (FDNs) in real time, delivering everything from hyper-realistic acoustic concert halls to pitch-shifted ambient 'shimmer' clouds that elevate solo guitars into symphonic orchestral soundscapes.
introduction.quote: Reverb is the acoustic environment your guitar inhabits. Without reverb, an electric guitar sounds like an anechoic test tone; with reverb, it sits in a sunlit cathedral, a smoky jazz club, or the boundless expanse of outer space.

sections.title: The Physical Mechanics of Reverb: Spring & Plate
sections.subtitle: The analog electromechanical transducers that defined vintage guitar tone

cards.title: Electromechanical Spring Reverb Tanks
cards.description: Pioneered by the Hammond Organ Company and immortalized by Leo Fender in 1963, a spring reverb tank uses a metal chassis containing two to four counter-wound steel springs. An electromagnetic input transducer converts the guitar signal into mechanical vibrations that travel down the springs. An output transducer at the opposite end converts the mechanical vibrations back into an electrical signal. Because sound waves travel much slower through coiled steel than through air, the reflections produce the signature splashy, boingy, metallic 'drip' that defined surf rock, reggae, and vintage country.

fields.label: Physical Mechanism
fields.value: Input coil driving 2 to 4 coiled steel springs picked up by an output induction coil

fields.label: Tonal Profile
fields.value: Bright, splashy, percussive, metallic 'boing' on hard pick attacks; warm decaying resonance

fields.label: Famous Origin
fields.value: Fender '63 Reverb Unit (standalone tube tank) and onboard Fender Blackface combos

fields.label: The 'Surf Drip'
fields.value: Muting a staccato note produces a distinct water-droplet slap that is the hallmark of surf guitar

items: Essential for Dick Dale surf rock, vintage rockabilly, dub reggae, and classic Fender blues tone
Sensitive to mechanical physical shock: kicking or bumping the amplifier creates thunderous crashing thunderclaps
Modern digital spring algorithms faithfully model the non-linear dispersion and metallic drip of physical tanks

cards.title: EMT 140 Suspended Studio Plate Reverb
cards.description: Engineered in Germany in 1957 by Elektro-Mess-Technik (EMT), the EMT 140 was the first artificial reverb to conquer high-end recording studios. A massive 1 x 2 meter sheet of cold-rolled steel (weighing nearly 600 lbs) was suspended under extreme tension inside a wooden cabinet. A central voice-coil driver vibrated the plate, and contact microphones picked up the vibrations. Unlike springs, plate reverb produces a dense, immediate, silky smooth diffuse decay with breathtaking high-frequency sparkle.

fields.label: Physical Mechanism
fields.value: Suspended tensioned steel sheet vibrated by an audio transducer and contact pickups

fields.label: Decay Character
fields.value: Ultra-dense, silky smooth late reflections without the boingy metallic flutter of springs

fields.label: High-End Sheen
fields.value: Naturally flatters vocals, snare drums, and lead guitar solos with shimmering presence

fields.label: Studio Benchmark
fields.value: The foundational reverb heard across Abbey Road (The Beatles, Pink Floyd) and 1970s rock

items: The premier reverb choice for melodic guitar solos: adds luxurious three-dimensional depth without cluttering the bass
Dampening pads adjusted the decay time mechanically from 0.5 to 5.0 seconds
Modern pedal DSP algorithms replicate the dense diffusion and sparkling top end of the EMT 140 in a compact box

sections.title: Algorithmic & Modern Digital Reverbs
sections.subtitle: How microprocessors simulate real-world spaces and craft surreal ambient soundscapes

cards.title: Room, Chamber & Hall Algorithms
cards.description: Algorithmic digital reverbs use complex feedback delay networks (FDNs) containing dozens of interconnected delay lines with micro-diffusers and low-pass damping filters to recreate real acoustic enclosures.

fields.label: Room Mode
fields.value: Short decay (0.4s–1.2s) with prominent early reflections; adds realistic studio air and intimate punch

fields.label: Chamber Mode
fields.value: Medium decay (1.5s–2.5s) with high diffusion; smooth, clear, classic 1950s echo chamber warmth

fields.label: Hall Mode
fields.value: Long decay (2.5s–6.0s) simulating symphony concert halls; expansive, lush, majestic depth

items: Room settings make dry electric guitar tracks sound like they were recorded in a world-class studio room
Hall settings provide luxurious, soaring sustain for slow ballad solos, emotional bends, and clean chord progressions

cards.title: Shimmer & Pitch-Shifted Cloud Reverb
cards.description: Pioneered in the 1980s by ambient producers Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois (using Lexicon and Eventide rack processors for U2's The Unforgettable Fire). Routes the decaying tail of a reverb back through a +1 octave pitch-shifter inside a feedback loop.

fields.label: The Shimmer Loop
fields.value: Reverb Tail → Octave-Up Pitch Shifter → Feedback Regeneration → Shimmering Cloud

fields.label: Sonic Texture
fields.value: Transforms single guitar chords into celestial, symphonic strings and angelic vocal pads

fields.label: Famous Users
fields.value: The Edge (U2), modern post-rock bands (Explosions in the Sky), modern worship guitarists

items: Allows a solo guitarist to fill a massive venue with lush, cinematic orchestral harmony
Pairing shimmer with a volume pedal creates seamless, bowed string swells and ambient film soundtrack textures

cards.title: Gated & Reverse Reverbs
cards.description: Specialized non-linear reverbs. Gated reverb cuts off the decaying tail abruptly with an electronic noise gate; Reverse reverb records incoming notes into a buffer and plays the decaying reflections backward in time.

fields.label: Gated Reverb
fields.value: Explosive, punchy initial burst that silences instantly; made famous in 1980s pop/rock

fields.label: Reverse Reverb
fields.value: Reflections swell backward from silence into a loud peak before the original note; surreal, dreamy wash

fields.label: Famous Origin
fields.value: Kevin Shields (My Bloody Valentine) using reverse reverb into high-gain fuzz on Loveless

items: Reverse reverb is the foundational acoustic cornerstone of the 1990s shoegaze and dream-pop movements
Gated reverb adds dramatic percussive impact to rhythm stabs without creating muddy ambient clutter

cards.title: Strymon BigSky
cards.description: The undisputed benchmark for ambient, studio, and worship guitarists. Powered by a high-performance SHARC DSP chip, BigSky houses 12 studio-grade reverb machines—including the iconic Cloud, Shimmer, Bloom, Plate, and Spring—300 preset memories, and full MIDI control.

fields.label: 12 Reverb Engines
fields.value: Room, Hall, Plate, Spring, Swell, Bloom, Cloud, Chorale, Shimmer, Magneto, Nonlinear, Reflections

fields.label: Cloud Machine
fields.value: Radically large, ultra-diffuse ambient cloud that turns simple notes into gorgeous orchestral pads

fields.label: Infinite / Freeze Hold
fields.value: Press and hold the active footswitch to sustain an ambient reverb chord indefinitely while soloing over it

fields.label: Hardware Features
fields.value: Ultra-low-noise 24-bit/96kHz converters, full stereo I/O, MIDI in/out, assignable expression routing

items: The industry benchmark standard found on almost every professional touring pedalboard in modern rock and ambient music
Independent Tone, Param, and Decay controls allow sculpting the exact frequency damping of the reverb tail
Analog dry-through ensures your original guitar signal never undergoes digital conversion

cards.title: Boss RV-6 Reverb
cards.description: The quintessential compact reverb workhorse. Driven by cutting-edge Boss DSP algorithms, the RV-6 features 8 versatile reverb modes—including lush Hall, realistic Spring, pristine Plate, Shimmer, and Dynamic (auto-ducking) reverb—with full stereo inputs and outputs.

fields.label: 8 Reverb Modes
fields.value: Hall, Plate, Room, Spring, Modulate, +Delay, Shimmer, and Dynamic

fields.label: Dynamic Ducking
fields.value: Automatically ducks reverb level while you play fast passages, blooming in full when you hold a note

fields.label: Expression Jack
fields.value: Connect an EV-5 expression pedal to control overall effect level with your foot in real time

fields.label: Stereo Routing
fields.value: True stereo inputs and outputs with auto-sensing mono/stereo switching

items: Modulate mode blends warm spatial chorus into a deep hall reverb for gorgeous 3D clean arpeggios
Shimmer mode adds pristine, musical octave-up sheen that never sounds shrill or harsh
Indestructible Boss compact metal enclosure built to survive decades of worldwide stage touring

cards.title: TC Electronic Hall of Fame 2
cards.description: A feature-packed digital reverb pedal featuring TC Electronic's groundbreaking MASH technology. The footswitch acts as a pressure-sensitive expression controller in real time, while TonePrint technology lets you beam custom artist presets wirelessly via your smartphone.

fields.label: MASH Technology
fields.value: Pressure-sensitive footswitch controls decay tail, shimmer intensity, or mix based on foot pressure

fields.label: 10 Reverb Types
fields.value: Room, Hall, Spring, Plate, Church, Shimmer, Mod, Lofi, and 3 custom TonePrint slots

fields.label: Shimmer Algorithm
fields.value: Co-developed with TC-Helicon; incorporates polyphonic octave pitch-shifting algorithm

items: True bypass or buffered bypass with analog dry-through preserves 100% pure guitar tone
Stereo I/O delivers expansive spatial imaging across two amplifiers or recording interfaces
TonePrint editor software lets you design your own signature reverbs from your computer or smartphone

cards.description: The simple, beloved compact reverb that helped launch the boutique digital pedal movement. Controlled by a single Reverb knob and a 3-way toggle switch (Spring, Hall, and the bizarre flanged 'Flerb'), it remains a staple on indie, garage, and alternative pedalboards.

fields.value: Single Reverb blend knob + 3-way slide switch (Spring, Hall, Flerb)

fields.label: Spring Algorithm
fields.value: Faithfully emulates the splashy, drippy character of vintage Fender spring reverb tanks

items: Minimalist single-knob design lets you dial in the perfect room space in under two seconds
The Spring setting produces authentic Dick Dale surf drip when picking hard near the guitar bridge
Die-cast chassis with true bypass to keep your clean tone completely uncolored when disengaged

cards.title: Strymon Flint
cards.description: The definitive tribute to the classic pairing of tube tremolo and vintage reverb found on legendary American amplifiers of the 1960s, 70s, and 80s. Houses three distinct historical reverb eras paired with three classic tremolo circuits.

fields.label: '60s Spring Reverb
fields.value: Faithful recreation of a full-size 2-spring tank with mechanical drip and splash

fields.label: '70s Electronic Plate
fields.value: Smooth, rich, multi-layered plate reverb simulating early studio digital plates

fields.label: '80s Rack Hall

fields.label: Dual Footswitches
fields.value: Independent bypass and controls for both Reverb and Tremolo sections

items: Allows re-ordering the signal path: run Tremolo into Reverb, or Reverb into Tremolo
The quintessential pedal for vintage soul, blues, surf rock, country twang, and indie pop
Ultra-low-noise 24-bit/96kHz processing with analog dry-through and full stereo inputs/outputs

cards.title: Fender '65 Princeton Reverb
cards.description: The legendary 12-watt all-tube combo amplifier featuring an authentic, tube-driven long-spring physical reverb tank. Powered by a 12AT7 tube driver and recovery circuit, the Princeton's physical spring reverb delivers the gold standard against which all digital pedals are measured.

fields.label: Physical Spring Tank
fields.value: Long 2-spring electromechanical tank mounted inside the bottom of the solid pine cabinet

fields.label: Tube Driver Circuit
fields.value: High-voltage 12AT7 tube driver transformer pushing the springs with genuine analog warmth

fields.label: Acoustic Interaction
fields.value: The speaker vibrating inside the pine cabinet acoustically feeds back into the springs, creating organic bloom

items: The most recorded small tube combo amplifier in music history, heard on countless blues, country, and pop records
Physical counter-wound springs produce genuine physical dispersion that digital algorithms strive to simulate
Integrated tube bias tremolo creates the warm, pulsing vibrato that defined 1960s rock recordings

sections.title: Dialing In Reverb: Pre-Delay & Frequency Clarity
sections.subtitle: Professional engineering techniques to keep your guitar articulate and prevent muddy clutter

cards.title: The Pre-Delay Secret: Protecting Your Pick Attack
cards.description: The number one cause of muddy, washed-out guitar tone is setting your reverb without sufficient Pre-Delay. Pre-Delay is the intentional gap of silence (in milliseconds) between when your pick strikes the string and when the diffuse reverb cloud begins to bloom. Without pre-delay, the reverb cloud immediately smothers the initial pick transient.

fields.label: Fast Lead Solos
fields.value: Set Pre-Delay to 30ms–50ms: Lets every picked note ring out with razor-sharp clarity before the reverb blooms

fields.label: Rhythm Chords
fields.value: Set Pre-Delay to 10ms–20ms: Adds natural acoustic room depth without dragging the rhythm tempo

fields.label: Ambient Swells
fields.value: Set Pre-Delay to 0ms: Dissolves the pick transient entirely for smooth, pad-like string washes

items: Separates the dry, punchy direct guitar note from the ambient space behind it
Allows you to use large, majestic hall reverbs without losing note articulation on fast blues and rock runs
Top studio engineers never mix reverb on guitars without fine-tuning pre-delay to match the song's tempo

cards.title: Signal Chain Placement & Effects Loop Mastery
cards.description: Because reverb simulates an acoustic room, it must sit at the very end of your pedalboard signal chain. Placing a high-gain distortion or fuzz pedal AFTER a reverb causes the distortion circuit to amplify and violently compress thousands of subtle reverb reflections simultaneously, turning your tone into an indecipherable roar of white noise.

fields.label: Pedalboard Golden Rule
fields.value: Guitar → Tuner → Wah → Overdrive/Distortion → Modulation → Delay → REVERB → Amp

fields.label: Using Amp Tube Distortion
fields.value: Place Reverb in your amplifier's EFFECTS LOOP (FX Send → Delay → Reverb → FX Return)

fields.label: The Shoegaze Exception
fields.value: Placing Reverb BEFORE Fuzz is an intentional experimental technique (pioneered by My Bloody Valentine) to create chaotic, textured walls of noise

items: Keeping Reverb at the end ensures that your delays and reverbs reflect your finished, polished guitar tone cleanly
In an amplifier's effects loop, reverb operates after the preamp tube distortion stages, keeping reflections crystal-clear
Always cut sub-100Hz low end on digital reverbs to avoid muddying the bass guitar and kick drum in live mixes
